body:
Blocked on [[T-111]] (the i18n layer). That ticket builds the machinery and
extracts the strings; this one decides WHICH languages ship and gets the
translations written. Deliberately separate: the layer is an engineering task,
this is a product decision plus per-language content.

## Language selection

Reference numbers — approximate share of internet users by preferred language;
sources vary a lot depending on whether they measure first language, "can use",
users vs population, or app-store revenue, so treat the shape as robust and the
digits as indicative:

  English ~26 · Chinese ~19 · Spanish ~8 · Arabic ~5 · Portuguese ~4 ·
  Indonesian ~4 · French ~3.5 · Japanese ~3 · Russian ~3 · German ~2 · Korean ~1.7

An en/fr/es/de/zh/ko/ja set — the intuitive "big app markets" list — reaches
roughly 60-65%, not 80%. Real 80% needs ~12 languages and must include
Portuguese, Arabic, Russian, Indonesian and Hindi. Korean is the weakest entry on
the intuitive list (~1.7%); Portuguese and Russian are each roughly double it and
are usually omitted.

But the denominator that matters here is not world internet users — it is people
who self-host a shopping list. That population reads English by construction
(GitHub, Docker, reverse proxies), and today it is the author. So:

1. **en, de** — the only two with actual users. German also stress-tests layouts
   hardest (compound nouns, 20-35% text expansion vs English).
2. **es, fr, pt-BR** — Latin script, large populations, near-zero marginal cost
   once the layer exists.
3. **zh-Hans, ja** — mechanical; no plurals, and text SHRINKS vs English, so
   layouts cannot break.
4. **ar, ru** — deliberate decisions, not defaults. See below.

## The two that are not just translation

- **Arabic is a layout task, not a translation task.** RTL means mirroring in
  Compose (`LayoutDirection`) and CSS logical properties. Decide yes/no BEFORE
  shipping the first non-English locale — retrofitting RTL is the expensive path.
- **Plurals are already handled** by the de-pluralization work, so ru and ar cost
  nothing extra on that axis (this was initially assessed the other way round —
  both platforms ship CLDR plural support anyway, and after de-pluralization the
  codebase needs none of it).

## Translation quality

Most of this app's copy is machine-translatable. These are not, and need someone
who has actually used the app:

- `backlog` as an item status (the wire values are `backlog`/`todo`/`checked`) —
  translates badly and inconsistently.
- "step-up password" (admin re-confirmation).
- "Shopping list" vs "Checklist" as list KINDS — the distinction must survive, and
  several languages use one word for both.
- Sync-health vocabulary: "quarantined"/"needs attention"/"pending".

## Not in scope

Wire values stay English identifiers (`backlog`/`todo`/`checked`,
`shopping`/`checklist`) — only their display localizes. Category names are
user-authored free text and are correctly NOT translatable: a German user types
German categories and it already works.
title: i18n: select shipping languages and write the translations
